problem: Prior image-goal navigation methods learn policies with RL inside simulators. They need millions of online interactions, ground-truth maps for reward shaping or distance supervision, and in NTS's case panoramic observations. This limits training to scanned 3D environments and creates a sim-to-real gap.
motivation: Building simulators and 3D assets is costly per scene, while passive egocentric videos of people or cameras roaming indoors are plentiful. The authors observe that the navigation state space is structured by a distance function: states that reduce distance-to-goal are better. A distance-to-goal estimator can therefore replace RL credit assignment and policy learning, and it can be learned from passive trajectories whose poses come from odometry or SLAM.
key_idea: Learn a graph-based geodesic distance-to-goal estimator and a target-in-sight predictor purely from passive RGB-D videos, then navigate greedily over an incrementally built topological map, using heuristic depth-based modules for obstacle avoidance and frontier expansion. No RL, no simulator interaction, no GT maps.
insight: Navigation can be cast as model-based greedy search on predicted distances. Passive videos supply enough supervision: distance along the non-optimal trajectory serves as the label, and depth-based heuristics handle local collision avoidance, which passive video cannot teach. On Gibson Straight-Easy, this beats DD-PPO trained with 5x more data and 10x more compute (68.00 vs 43.20 SR). The GT-substitution ablations (Tab. 3, Gibson) locate the bottlenecks. Replacing the heuristic explorable-area module with GT costs almost nothing (e.g., Straight-Easy 99.90 vs 100.00 SR). Using the learned target/stop predictor G_T instead of GT drops Straight-Easy SR from 99.90 to 79.40 and Curved-Easy from 99.70 to 65.00. Using the learned distance network G_D instead of GT causes the largest drops on long and curved episodes: Straight-Hard 62.16 to 23.45 and Curved-Easy 65.00 to 35.50. Distance prediction over large search spaces is therefore the main limiting factor. Training on real YouTube tours (RealEstate10K) degrades performance versus sim-rendered videos because of domain shift and shorter trajectories, yet still beats BC baselines.
method: Topological map G(N,E): nodes carry poses and are either explored (with stored RGB-D image) or unexplored frontier nodes; edges carry relative pose (flattened 4x4 transform) between adjacent nodes.

Distance network G_D (global policy): ResNet-18 encodes explored-node images into 512-d features. Unexplored nodes get zero features. Two GAT layers, extended to use edge (pose) features in the attention coefficients, propagate features to unexplored nodes. Each node feature is concatenated with the goal-image feature and passed to an MLP (512-256-1) with a sigmoid that predicts a clipped inverse distance score 1-min(d,30)/30. Training uses MSE on unexplored nodes only.
Greedy sub-goal selection: the next sub-goal is the unexplored node minimizing predicted distance-to-goal plus travel cost, where travel cost is the shortest path on G from the current node.

Heuristic local policy G_LP: the point-nav controller from Active Neural SLAM. It builds a temporary local metric map from depth and (noisy) pose to reach the sub-goal (rho, phi) with FORWARD 0.25m / TURN 15° actions, and the map is discarded after each sub-goal.

Explorable-area module G_EA (untrained): tests 9 directions [0, ±15, ±30, ±45, ±60]° in the depth image for obstacles within 3 m. It adds unexplored nodes 1 m away in free directions, or only an edge if a nearby node already exists.

Target prediction G_T (stop criterion): an MLP on the Hadamard product of projected ResNet-18 features of the current and goal images. It predicts a goal-in-sight probability (BCE) plus goal distance and direction (Smooth-L1). If probability > 0.5, the agent navigates to the predicted goal location and stops.

Passive-data training pipeline: step-wise video frames with odometry are clustered via affinity propagation (Places365 ResNet-18 features + pose) into topological graphs and expanded with G_EA frontier nodes. Sub-graphs and goal nodes are sampled uniformly, with distance along the trajectory as the label (~1k instances per scan). Adjacent node pairs serve as positives for G_T.

setting.backbone: ResNet-18 image encoder + 2-layer edge-feature Graph Attention Network + MLP heads (trained on passive videos); heuristic depth-based local policy and explorable-area module
setting.model_size: not stated (ResNet-18 encoder + 2 GAT layers of 512-d + small MLPs)
setting.training_data: Passive RGB-D trajectory videos with odometry, no actions or rewards. Habitat-rendered videos built from concatenated shortest paths between 2-4 random points: 19K videos / ~1M frames on Gibson train scenes and 43K videos / ~2.5M frames on MP3D train scenes, with sensor/actuation noise injected in the noisy setting. Alternative: RealEstate10K YouTube real-estate tours (80K clips, ~10M frames, SLAM poses). G_D is trained with ~1k instances per scan.
setting.observation: egocentric narrow-FOV (120°) RGB-D 480x640 + 3x1 odometry pose (GT or noisy) + RGB goal image
setting.action_space: high-level: topological-graph sub-goal nodes (1 m frontier); low-level: FORWARD 0.25 m / TURN LEFT/RIGHT 15° / STOP
setting.simulator: Habitat (evaluation only; also used to render passive training videos, but no interaction during training)
setting.privileged: GT pose and deterministic actuation in the 'w/out noise' setting (a noisy pose + actuation variant is also reported); none otherwise

numbers_note: Results are reported only per path type (straight/curved) and per difficulty (easy/medium/hard); there is no overall aggregate SR/SPL. Metric keys therefore encode setting as SR_<type>_<difficulty>. Episodes are the paper's own (~1000 per setting sampled from the test scenes, narrow 120° FOV), so the numbers are not comparable to standard panoramic ImageNav benchmarks such as NTS or Mezghani et al. There are two internal inconsistencies. Gibson Straight-Hard for the full NRNS is 23.82/18.28 in Table 1 but 23.45/18.84 in the ablation Table 3. The 'BC w/ ResNet + GRU' row in Table 4 (Gibson) repeats the MP3D numbers (30.20/29.57), not Table 1's Gibson numbers (34.90/33.43). GT-substitution ablation rows (Tables 3 and MP3D appendix) are omitted here because they use oracle modules. The checklist claims error bars were reported, but none appear in the NRNS tables; only the RL baseline results are averaged over 3 seeds.
results: Trained only on passive videos, NRNS outperforms all BC and DD-PPO RL baselines on SR on Gibson and MP3D image-goal navigation. The RL baselines include one trained with 5x more data and 10x more compute (100M steps). On Gibson, NRNS reaches 68.00 SR / 61.62 SPL on Straight-Easy versus 43.20 / 38.54 for the strongest RL baseline and 34.90 / 33.43 for BC ResNet+GRU. On Straight-Hard it reaches 23.82 SR versus 7.44 for RL. On MP3D Straight-Easy it reaches 64.70 SR versus 36.40 for RL. RL still has higher SPL on some curved settings (e.g., Gibson Curved-Medium 18.52 vs 12.08). Adding sensor/actuation noise costs only 0.8-8 SR points on Gibson and 1-5 on MP3D. Training on real-world RealEstate10K videos lowers performance (Gibson Straight-Easy 56.42 SR) but still beats the BC baselines.
limitations: The narrow-FOV greedy policy struggles on curved and hard episodes (e.g., Gibson Curved-Hard 12.50 SR, very low SPL). GT-substitution ablations show the learned distance network and the learned stop predictor are the dominant error sources.

Evaluation is simulation-only, with no real robot, on the paper's own episode splits, so results are not comparable to standard ImageNav benchmarks. Most passive training videos are themselves rendered from Habitat shortest-path trajectories rather than real footage.

Distance labels come from non-optimal trajectories and overestimate true geodesic distance. The method relies on depth, odometry, and heuristic modules, and real-world RealEstate10K training suffers a domain gap (shorter clips, different motion).
